title: Computing Mean Squared Error (MSE) for 1D Linear Regression
description: Define mse(theta0, theta1, X, y) to compute y_hat = theta0 + theta1 * X[:, 0] and np.mean((y_hat - y)**2), then evaluate it at theta0 = 0, theta1 = 0.

steps.description: Define `mse(theta0, theta1, X, y)` to compute linear predictions `y_hat = theta0 + theta1 * X[:, 0]` and return the average squared residual `np.mean((y_hat - y)**2)`.
Call `mse(0, 0, X, y)` and print the baseline mean squared error when both intercept and slope are zero.
Look at lines 3-4: `y_hat - y` forms the vector of residuals for all `n` points, squaring `(y_hat - y)**2` makes every residual non-negative, and `np.mean(...)` averages them.

steps.question: When `theta0 = 0` and `theta1 = 0` in `mse(0, 0, X, y)`, what is `y_hat` on line 3, and what does `np.mean((y_hat - y)**2)` simplify to?
steps.answer: `y_hat` is a vector of all zeros, so `np.mean((0 - y)**2)` simplifies to `np.mean(y**2)` (`64.45133245844147`).

steps.description: Inside `mse(0, 0, X, y)`, line 3 computes `y_hat = 0 + 0 * X[:, 0]` (an array of 100 zeros).
Line 4 returns `np.mean((y_hat - y)**2)` (`64.45133245844147`), which line 6 prints.
